title: Keep the review moving.
intro: The brief was to make Change Stack easier to use without losing what it can do. I focused on understanding a change, checking the code and keeping my place. Developer exploration exposed a mistake in my first version: I had removed useful signals while simplifying the screen. This revision responds to that feedback. It is not a completed usability study.
sections: I restored layer numbers, file counts, additions, deletions and recorded severity. Layers start compact; expanding files and opening a layer are separate actions. The first context view explains the file, shows the captured finding’s status and leaves summaries collapsed. Complexity, severity and resolution keep their own labels.

Opening a summary reveals the explanation without moving the code. Statement links take you to specific lines; the whole range and source wording remain available. Inspect and Return preserve the caller’s position. The original already scrolls through files within a layer. I extended that stream across layers. Modified files keep equal Before/After panes; added files use the full width, as in the source. Deletions and unchanged context remain available.

Overview holds the pinned PR context, source-ordered layers and recorded findings. Severity filters narrow this table without reordering the review. A small curated permission-check path links to workspace access, tenant resolution and record ownership. Return restores the previous reading position.
Keep state clear and code readable

Viewed is the primary progress count. Summary Seen is separate; scrolling changes neither. Major · Resolved reads as history. Range notes retain their file, side and lines, and stay local. Reviewing controls take 92 px. Light, Dark and System use semantic colors; switching themes preserves drafts and position. Dark colors are derived, not claimed as captured product tokens.
limits: All 52 pinned diffs (+5,722 / −127), their layer membership and comparison base are verified. Live Split behavior informed the final layout. Summary and thread coverage is partial; semantic outlines, blame and other secondary tools remain previews. The source uses both Trivial and Nitpick; I keep those labels rather than silently treating them as identical. Narrow highlights can hide context, so whole ranges stay available.
next: Next I’d compare the same permission-review task in both versions: explain the checks, inspect the guard, return and leave a range note. I’d record missed checks, lost position and help needed. I haven’t measured faster or more accurate reviews.
